lesson.title: Why Nothing In Biology Is Free: An Introduction to Thermodynamics
lesson.summary: Thermodynamics is the study of energy and how it moves and changes form, and it sets the basic rules that every living process, from muscle contraction to photosynthesis, has to obey.
lesson.body:
Every living thing is, among other things, a machine for handling energy. Muscles contract, nerves fire, plants build sugar out of sunlight and carbon dioxide, and none of it happens for free. Thermodynamics is the branch of physics that describes how energy behaves, how it moves from one place to another, how it converts from one form to another, such as light energy into chemical energy, and what limits govern those conversions. Biology did not invent its own separate set of energy rules. Every living cell obeys the same thermodynamic laws that govern a steam engine or a star, which is part of why thermodynamics belongs at the foundation of any serious study of biology.

To talk about thermodynamics precisely, it helps to define a system and its surroundings. The system is whatever part of the universe is under consideration, which could be as small as a single cell or as large as an entire forest, and the surroundings are everything else. Biological systems are almost always open systems, meaning they exchange both energy and matter with their surroundings: an animal cell takes in nutrients and oxygen and releases carbon dioxide and heat, and a plant cell takes in light energy, water, and carbon dioxide and releases oxygen and sugar. This constant exchange is not incidental, it is required, because as later sections will show, living systems are built and maintained in ways that only make sense with a continuous outside supply of usable energy.

One especially important form of energy in biology is called free energy, the portion of a system's total energy that is actually available to do useful work, such as building a molecule, moving a flagellum, or pumping an ion across a membrane. Not all energy in a system is usable in this way, and understanding exactly why some energy is available and some is not requires two more ideas that build directly on thermodynamics: the first law, which tracks how much total energy exists, and the second law, which explains why not all of it can be put to work.

Thermodynamics also introduces a vocabulary that recurs constantly in biology: heat, work, and energy itself. Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference, work is energy transferred by some organized, directed process, such as a molecular motor pulling on a filament, and energy in general is simply the capacity to do work. A cell cannot use heat directly to do biological work the way it uses chemical or mechanical energy, which is one reason cells are so heavily invested in molecules, especially ATP, that store and release energy in controlled, usable packets rather than as diffuse heat.

The reason thermodynamics comes first in this sequence of concepts is that it is not really biology at all, it is physics that biology cannot escape. Every reaction inside a cell, every transport process across a membrane, every muscle twitch, has to be consistent with how energy is conserved and how it disperses. The next few sections build directly on this foundation, first by pinning down exactly how energy is conserved, then by explaining why energy tends to spread out rather than stay concentrated, and finally by combining both ideas into a single quantity, free energy, that predicts whether a biological process can happen on its own at all.
